answers.question: Explain how a production REST API handles the five concerns that interviewers probe together — structured error handling (RFC 9457 Problem Details with correct status codes), pagination for large result sets (why cursor/keyset beats offset at depth), API versioning (URL path, header, media-type), idempotency (idempotent HTTP methods plus the Idempotency-Key header for safe retries of POST), and content negotiation (the Accept and Content-Type headers choosing JSON vs XML) — and show how they fit together in real finance code.
answers.shortTitle: REST API — error handling, pagination, versioning, idempotency, content negotiation

s1_definition.profdef: A production REST API treats every business thing as a resource with a stable URL and acts on it using the standard HTTP methods and status codes. Error handling returns a consistent machine-readable body, ideally RFC 9457 Problem Details, with the correct status code rather than a vague 200 plus an error flag. Pagination splits large collections into pages; offset pagination uses LIMIT and OFFSET and degrades at deep pages, while cursor (keyset) pagination remembers the last key seen and seeks forward, staying fast at any depth. API versioning lets the contract evolve without breaking old clients, commonly through a URL path segment such as /api/v1, a custom header, or a media-type. Idempotency means making the same request twice has the same effect as making it once; GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent by definition, and POST is made safely retryable with a client-supplied Idempotency-Key. Content negotiation uses the Accept and Content-Type headers so the same endpoint can serve or accept JSON or XML.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India's online system as a very disciplined bank branch. Error handling is the printed rejection slip that always has the same layout, a clear reason, and the right stamp, so Rajesh's mobile app always knows how to read it. Pagination is how the clerk hands you the account statement in neat pages instead of one impossibly long roll — and a smart clerk remembers "last entry you saw was number 500" instead of recounting from the top every time. Versioning is like the bank keeping the old form (v1) valid for existing customers while rolling out a new form (v2) for everyone else. Idempotency is the guarantee that if Rajesh taps "Transfer" twice because his network glitched, the money only moves once. Content negotiation is the clerk asking "do you want this in English or Hindi?" and giving you the format you asked for.
s1_definition.oneliner: A production REST API returns consistent Problem Details errors with correct status codes, paginates with cursors for deep pages, versions its contract, uses Idempotency-Keys so retried POSTs run once, and negotiates JSON or XML through Accept and Content-Type.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A production REST API treats every business thing as a resource with a stable URL and acts on it using the standard HTTP methods and status codes. Error handling returns a consistent machine-readable body, ideally RFC 9457 Problem Details, with the correct status code rather than a vague 200 plus an error flag. API versioning lets the contract evolve without breaking old clients, commonly through a URL path segment such as /api/v1, a custom header, or a media-type. Idempotency means making the same request twice has the same effect as making it once; GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent by definition, and POST is made safely retryable with a client-supplied Idempotency-Key. Content negotiation uses the Accept and Content-Type headers so the same endpoint can serve or accept JSON or XML.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India's online system as a very disciplined bank branch. Error handling is the printed rejection slip that always has the same layout, a clear reason, and the right stamp, so Rajesh's mobile app always knows how to read it. sections.s2_technical:
Let me walk through each of the five concerns the way an experienced engineer would explain it to a junior joining the payments team, with a small finance code snippet for each so you can see the API actually being used.

Error handling is the first thing that separates a toy API from a production one. The anti-pattern is returning 200 OK with a body like a success flag set to false, because every client then has to parse the body to know whether the call worked, and HTTP caches and monitoring treat a failure as a success. The correct approach is to return the right status code — 404 when a fund does not exist, 400 for bad input, 409 for a conflict — with a consistent RFC 9457 Problem Details body. In Spring you build it directly: `ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Account not found: SAV9999"); pd.setTitle("Account Not Found"); pd.setProperty("accountId", "SAV9999");`. A single `@RestControllerAdvice` class with `@ExceptionHandler` methods turns each domain exception into one of these bodies, so the controller code stays clean and every error looks identical to the client.

Pagination matters the moment a collection grows. Offset pagination is the obvious approach — `SELECT * FROM transactions ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000` — but the database still has to walk and discard one hundred thousand rows before returning the next twenty, so page five thousand is painfully slow and new inserts can shift rows between pages. Cursor (keyset) pagination fixes this by remembering the last key seen and querying forward from it: `SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE id > :lastId ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`. Because the id column is indexed, the database seeks straight to that point, so the ten-thousandth page is as fast as the first. The API returns a `nextCursor` value that the client sends back to fetch the following page, for example `GET /api/v1/transactions?cursor=TXN-100020&limit=20`.

API versioning lets you change the contract without breaking existing integrations. The most common and most visible approach is a path segment: `GET /api/v1/accounts/SAV2001` today and `GET /api/v2/accounts/SAV2001` when the response shape changes. In Spring you simply map the controllers accordingly: `@RequestMapping("/api/v1/accounts")` on one controller and `@RequestMapping("/api/v2/accounts")` on another. Other styles exist — a custom header such as `X-API-Version: 2` or a versioned media-type like `Accept: application/vnd.bank.v2+json` — but path versioning is the easiest for clients to see and for you to route. The senior point is that v1 must keep working unchanged for as long as customers depend on it.

Idempotency is about making retries safe. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent by definition: reading an account twice, replacing it with the same body twice, or deleting it twice leaves the server in the same final state. POST is not idempotent by default — posting a transfer twice would move the money twice. The industry solution is an `Idempotency-Key` header: the client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it, for example `Idempotency-Key: 7f3b-rajesh-rent-oct`. The server stores the key with the result of the first request; if the same key arrives again, it returns the stored result instead of processing the transfer again. In code this is a check at the top of the handler: `if (idempotencyStore.containsKey(key)) return idempotencyStore.get(key);` before doing the work, then saving the result under that key.

Content negotiation lets one endpoint serve multiple formats. The client states what it wants with the `Accept` header and what it is sending with the `Content-Type` header. If Rajesh's app sends `Accept: application/xml`, Spring serializes the response as XML; if it sends `Accept: application/json`, it returns JSON — the controller code does not change. You enable this by declaring the produced types: `@GetMapping(value = "/{id}", produces = {MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE})`. Spring's `HttpMessageConverter` chain then picks the right converter based on the Accept header. A senior nuance is that if the client asks for a format you cannot produce, you return 406 Not Acceptable rather than silently defaulting.
sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the real situation at National Bank of India before we look at any code, the way I would explain it to a friend who understands banking but not Java.

The bank runs a REST API that powers its mobile app and internet banking site. Customers like Rajesh, a software engineer with savings account SAV2001, and Priya, a property owner with current account CUR3001, use it to look up accounts, read their transaction history, and move money. The API started simple but is now used by millions of customers, and five separate production problems have forced the team to do things the right way.

Problem 1 — When something goes wrong, the app shows confusing messages. The old API returned 200 OK with a body that sometimes said success was false, so the app could not tell a real failure from a real success, and the monitoring dashboards were useless because every call looked like a success. This is exactly why we return proper status codes with RFC 9457 Problem Details: a missing account returns 404 with a structured body, bad input returns 400, and the app always knows how to display the error.

Problem 2 — Rajesh has fifteen years of transactions, and scrolling to the oldest ones used to take forever. The old API used offset pagination, so fetching page five thousand made the database count and throw away a hundred thousand rows every time. This is exactly why we switch to cursor pagination: the API remembers the last transaction id shown and fetches the next batch starting just after it, so deep pages load instantly.

Problem 3 — The bank wants to change the shape of the account response to add new fields and rename an old one, but it cannot break the thousands of existing app installs still on the old version. This is exactly why we use URL path versioning: the old clients keep calling /api/v1 and get the old shape, while new clients call /api/v2 and get the improved shape.

Problem 4 — Rajesh taps "Pay Rent" on a weak train network, the response is slow, and he taps again. Without protection the bank would transfer his rent twice. This is exactly why we use an Idempotency-Key: the app sends a unique key for that rent payment, and if the same key arrives twice the server returns the first result instead of moving the money again.

Problem 5 — One partner integration consumes XML while the mobile app consumes JSON, and the bank does not want to maintain two separate endpoints. This is exactly why we use content negotiation: the same endpoint serves JSON or XML depending on the Accept header the caller sends.

Now that the problems are clear, here is what each part of the code will do. The Account and Transaction classes are the domain objects. The AccountResponse record is the versioned DTO returned to clients. The AccountNotFoundException and a global handler produce Problem Details error bodies. The PageResponse record carries a page of transactions plus the next cursor. The IdempotencyStore remembers keys and their results. The BankApiService holds the logic: getAccount reads one account, listTransactions does cursor pagination, and transfer applies the idempotency check. The demo wires it all together and prints the output so you can see each concern in action.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile the single-file runnable demo
javac BankApiDemo.java

# Run it
java com.bank.api.BankApiDemo

# In a real Spring Boot project you would build and run the jar instead:
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/bank-rest-api-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev

# Versioning: v1 and v2 live side by side
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/SAV2001 -H 'Accept: application/json'
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v2/accounts/SAV2001 -H 'Accept: application/json'

# Content negotiation: same endpoint, XML instead of JSON
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v2/accounts/SAV2001 -H 'Accept: application/xml'

# Cursor pagination: follow the nextCursor from the previous page
curl 'http://localhost:8080/api/v2/accounts/SAV2001/transactions?limit=2'
curl 'http://localhost:8080/api/v2/accounts/SAV2001/transactions?cursor=TXN-00002&limit=2'

# Idempotency: retrying with the same key moves money only once
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v2/transfers \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Idempotency-Key: 7f3b-rajesh-rent-oct' \
  -d '{"from":"SAV2001","to":"CUR3001","amount":50000}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a sequence of real API calls: read Rajesh's account, read a missing account, page through Rajesh's transactions two at a time, and transfer fifty thousand rupees twice with the same idempotency key.

Step 1 — The app calls getAccount for SAV2001. The service reads the account from the repository, finds Rajesh with a balance of ten lakh rupees, and builds a v2 AccountResponse DTO containing only the account id, the holder name, and the balance. The internal version column stays hidden. The output is a clean 200-equivalent object.

Step 2 — The app calls getAccount for SAV9999. The repository returns null, so the service throws an AccountNotFoundException. In a real API this becomes a 404 response with an RFC 9457 Problem Details body carrying a type, a title, a status of 404, a detail message, and the offending account id. The data here is an error object, not a money change.

Step 3 — The app requests the first page of transactions with no cursor and a limit of two. The repository seeks from the start and returns TXN-00001 and TXN-00002. The service sets the next cursor to TXN-00002 and marks hasMore as true. The output is page one plus the cursor the client must send next.

Step 4 — The app requests the next page, sending cursor TXN-00002 and limit two. The repository seeks strictly past TXN-00002 and returns TXN-00003 and TXN-00004. Notice the database never re-reads the first two rows — that is the whole point of cursor pagination. The output is page two plus the new cursor.

Step 5 — The app calls transfer with idempotency key 7f3b-rajesh-rent-oct for fifty thousand rupees from SAV2001 to CUR3001. The key is not in the store, so the service debits Rajesh (his balance becomes nine lakh fifty thousand) and credits Priya (her balance becomes three lakh), creates transfer id TXF-00001, and saves that id under the key. The output is TXF-00001.

Step 6 — The app retries the same transfer with the same key because the network glitched. This time the service finds the key already present and returns the stored TXF-00001 immediately, without touching any balance. Rajesh is debited only once. The output is the same TXF-00001, proving idempotency.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In our banking REST API I treat five concerns as non-negotiable, because together they are what makes an API production-grade rather than a demo. The first is error handling. I never return 200 OK with a success-false flag, because that blinds both clients and monitoring. Instead I return the correct status code — 404 for a missing account, 400 for bad input, 409 for a conflict — with a consistent RFC 9457 Problem Details body built in one @RestControllerAdvice class, so every error the mobile app receives looks identical and is easy to display.

The second is pagination. For Rajesh with fifteen years of transactions, offset pagination is a trap because the database walks and discards every earlier row, so deep pages crawl. I use cursor, or keyset, pagination: the client sends the last transaction id it saw and the query does WHERE id greater than that cursor with an index seek, so page ten thousand is as fast as page one. The response carries a nextCursor the client sends back for the following page.

The third is versioning, which I usually do with a URL path segment so v1 and v2 live side by side and I can evolve the response shape without breaking the thousands of app installs still on the old version. The fourth is idempotency. GET, PUT, and DELETE are naturally idempotent, but POST is not, so for transfers I require an Idempotency-Key header. The server stores the result against that key, and if Rajesh double-taps Pay Rent on a flaky network the retry returns the stored transfer id and the money moves exactly once.

The fifth is content negotiation. One endpoint serves our JSON mobile app and an XML partner integration by honouring the Accept header, and if a client asks for a format we cannot produce we return 406 rather than silently guessing. When I explain this to an interviewer I stress that each of these came from a real production pain — confusing error screens, slow deep pages, a breaking contract change, a double-charged customer, and a partner that needed XML — and that getting all five right is what lets a banking API scale to millions of customers without surprises.

answers.question: Explain the key design patterns and principles used in a production banking service — the five SOLID principles, the Strategy pattern for swapping algorithms, the Builder pattern for constructing complex objects, the Observer pattern for event-driven reactions, the Circuit Breaker pattern for protecting against failing downstream systems, and the DTO pattern for separating the API contract from the internal entity — and show how they fit together in real finance code.
answers.shortTitle: Design Patterns — SOLID, Strategy, Builder, Observer, Circuit Breaker, DTO

s1_definition.profdef: Design patterns are proven, reusable solutions to recurring design problems. The Strategy pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface so behaviour can be selected at runtime. The Builder pattern constructs a complex object step by step instead of through a large constructor. The Observer pattern lets one event notify many independent listeners without the publisher knowing who they are. The Circuit Breaker pattern stops calling a failing downstream dependency after a threshold of errors, failing fast and allowing recovery. The DTO (Data Transfer Object) pattern carries data across a boundary, decoupling the public API shape from the internal persistence entity. SOLID is the five object-oriented design principles — Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion — that keep code maintainable and testable.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India as a well-run branch. The Strategy pattern is like having different fee clerks for regular, premium, and promotional customers — the manager just calls "the right clerk for this customer" without a giant rulebook. The Builder pattern is like filling a loan application form field by field instead of shouting fifteen details at once to a hurried clerk. The Observer pattern is like ringing one bell when a transfer completes, and the audit desk, the SMS desk, and the dashboard desk all react on their own. The Circuit Breaker is like the branch temporarily putting up a "counter closed" sign when the central server keeps timing out, so customers are not stuck in an endless queue. The DTO pattern is the printed receipt you hand to Rajesh — it shows what he is allowed to see, not the bank's full internal ledger row. SOLID is the branch's operating manual that keeps every desk doing exactly one job cleanly.
s1_definition.oneliner: Strategy swaps behaviour behind an interface, Builder assembles complex objects readably, Observer fans out one event to many listeners, Circuit Breaker fails fast on a sick dependency, DTO shields the API from the entity, and SOLID is the five rules that hold it all together.

The Strategy pattern is like having different fee clerks for regular, premium, and promotional customers — the manager just calls "the right clerk for this customer" without a giant rulebook. The Builder pattern is like filling a loan application form field by field instead of shouting fifteen details at once to a hurried clerk. The Observer pattern is like ringing one bell when a transfer completes, and the audit desk, the SMS desk, and the dashboard desk all react on their own. The Circuit Breaker is like the branch temporarily putting up a "counter closed" sign when the central server keeps timing out, so customers are not stuck in an endless queue. The DTO pattern is the printed receipt you hand to Rajesh — it shows what he is allowed to see, not the bank's full internal ledger row. SOLID is the branch's operating manual that keeps every desk doing exactly one job cleanly.

**One line to remember:** Strategy swaps behaviour behind an interface, Builder assembles complex objects readably, Observer fans out one event to many listeners, Circuit Breaker fails fast on a sick dependency, DTO shields the API from the entity, and SOLID is the five rules that hold it all together.

sections.s2_technical:
Let me walk through each pattern the way an experienced engineer would explain it to a junior joining the payments team, with a small finance code snippet for each so you can see it actually being used.

The Strategy pattern replaces a long if-else or switch chain over "what kind of thing is this" with a set of small classes that all implement one interface. In our bank, fee calculation differs by customer tier, so we define a `FeeStrategy` interface with a `calculateFee` method and keep each variant in its own class. We register them in a Map and pick one by name at runtime: `FeeStrategy strategy = feeStrategies.get("premium"); BigDecimal fee = strategy.calculateFee(new BigDecimal("50000"));`. Adding a festival "zero fee" promotion means writing one new class and adding one Map entry, with zero edits to the existing fee logic.

The Builder pattern constructs an object that has many fields, some optional, without a constructor that takes fifteen arguments in a fixed order. For a transfer record you write `TransferResult result = TransferResult.builder().transferId("TXF-00001").from("SAV2001").to("CUR3001").amount(new BigDecimal("50000")).status("COMPLETED").build();`. Each call reads like a sentence, optional fields can simply be skipped, and the object can be made immutable because all fields are set before `build` returns it.

The Observer pattern decouples an event from the things that react to it. When a transfer settles, several independent actions must happen: write an audit record, send an SMS, update a dashboard. Instead of the transfer code calling each one directly, it publishes a single event and the listeners react on their own. In Spring this is `applicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(new TransferCompletedEvent("TXF-00001"));` and each listener is an `@EventListener` method such as `@EventListener void onCompleted(TransferCompletedEvent e) { auditService.record(e.transferId()); }`. Adding a new reaction, like a fraud re-check, means adding one listener class and never touching the transfer code.

The Circuit Breaker pattern protects your service from a downstream dependency that has become slow or unavailable. When the bank calls an external exchange-rate API and it starts timing out, continuing to call it ties up threads and makes everything slow. A circuit breaker counts failures, and once they cross a threshold it "opens" and immediately returns a fallback instead of calling the sick dependency. With Resilience4j you annotate the call: `@CircuitBreaker(name = "fxRate", fallbackMethod = "cachedRate") public BigDecimal liveRate(String pair) { ... }`, and the fallback `private BigDecimal cachedRate(String pair, Throwable t) { return lastKnownRate.get(pair); }` returns the last cached rate. After a wait the breaker moves to "half-open" and lets a trial call through to check if the dependency has recovered.

The DTO pattern separates the data you expose at the API boundary from the entity you store in the database. The `Account` entity has internal columns like an optimistic-lock version and an internal risk score that customers must never see. So the controller returns an `AccountResponse` DTO built from the entity: `return new AccountResponse(account.getAccountId(), account.getHolderName(), account.getBalance());`. This shields internal fields, lets the API evolve independently of the schema, and avoids accidentally serializing a lazy JPA relationship.

Now SOLID, the five principles that make all of the above clean. Single Responsibility means each class does one job: `TransferService` moves money, `AuditService` records history, `NotificationService` sends messages — not one giant class doing all three. Open/Closed means the system is open to new behaviour but closed to editing working code; the Strategy Map achieves this because a new fee type is a new class, never an edit to existing logic. Liskov Substitution means any `FeeStrategy` implementation works correctly wherever the interface is expected, so swapping `RegularFeeStrategy` for `PremiumFeeStrategy` never breaks the caller. Interface Segregation means you keep interfaces small and focused — a `FeeStrategy` only computes fees rather than being forced to implement unrelated methods. Dependency Inversion means `TransferService` depends on the `FeeStrategy` interface, not a concrete class, which is exactly why you can inject a mock in a unit test: `new TransferService(repo, Map.of("regular", new RegularFeeStrategy()))`. A senior-level nuance is that these patterns reinforce each other — Strategy plus a Map registry is literally how you implement Open/Closed and Dependency Inversion at the same time.
sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the real situation at National Bank of India before we look at any code, the way I would explain it to a friend who understands banking but not Java.

The bank runs a money-transfer service. Customers like Rajesh, a software engineer with savings account SAV2001 holding ten lakh rupees, and Priya, a property owner with current account CUR3001 holding two lakh fifty thousand rupees, move money between accounts every day. On top of the transfer itself the bank charges a fee, sends notifications, writes an audit trail, and sometimes needs a live currency rate from an external service. The code behind all of this grew messy over the years, and the team wants to clean it up using proper design patterns.

Problem 1 — The fee depends on the customer tier, and the rules keep changing. A regular customer pays one percent, a premium customer like Rajesh pays half a percent, and during festival promotions the fee is waived entirely. The old code was one enormous if-else block inside the transfer method, and every new promotion meant editing that live, working method and risking a bug in real money calculations. This is exactly what the Strategy pattern solves: each fee rule becomes its own small class behind a common interface, and the service simply looks up the correct one by name, so a new promotion is a new class plus one registry entry.

Problem 2 — Building the result object is clumsy. A transfer result has an id, a from-account, a to-account, an amount, a fee, a status, and a timestamp, and some of these are optional in failure cases. Passing all of them into one constructor in a fixed order led to bugs where the from and to accounts were accidentally swapped. This is exactly what the Builder pattern solves: each field is set by name in a readable chain, so nobody confuses the order.

Problem 3 — When a transfer completes, many things must happen, and the list keeps growing. Today it is an audit record and an SMS; tomorrow it is a dashboard update and a loyalty-points credit. If the transfer method calls each one directly, that method becomes a dumping ground and every new reaction risks breaking the core money movement. This is exactly what the Observer pattern solves: the transfer publishes one "transfer completed" event, and independent listeners each react on their own.

Problem 4 — The bank sometimes needs a live foreign-exchange rate from an external provider, and that provider occasionally goes down or becomes very slow. When it does, transfer threads pile up waiting for a response that never comes, and the whole service grinds to a halt. This is exactly what the Circuit Breaker pattern solves: after too many failures it stops calling the sick provider and instantly returns the last known cached rate, protecting the rest of the system.

Problem 5 — The API must never leak internal columns. The account row in the database has an internal version number and a risk score that are bank secrets. This is exactly what the DTO pattern solves: the controller returns a trimmed response object containing only the fields the customer is allowed to see.

Now that the problems are clear, here is what each part of the code will do. The `FeeStrategy` interface defines the fee contract, with `RegularFeeStrategy`, `PremiumFeeStrategy`, and `ZeroFeeStrategy` as implementations registered in a Map. The `Account` class is the domain object with `debit` and `credit` methods. The `TransferResult` class uses a Builder to assemble the outcome. The `TransferCompletedEvent` plus the audit and notification listeners demonstrate the Observer pattern. The `FxRateClient` shows a simple circuit breaker protecting an external call. The `AccountResponse` record is the DTO returned to the customer. The `TransferService` ties them together, and `TransferDemo` runs the whole flow so you can see the output.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a request to transfer fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh's savings account SAV2001 to Priya's current account CUR3001, with Rajesh on the premium tier.

Step 1 — The service receives the call with fromId SAV2001, toId CUR3001, amount fifty thousand, and tier premium. At this point the data lives only in method parameters and nothing has changed in any account.

Step 2 — The repository loads both accounts. Rajesh is read with a balance of ten lakh rupees, and Priya is read with a balance of two lakh fifty thousand rupees. The data is now in memory as two Account objects, still unchanged.

Step 3 — The Strategy pattern picks the fee rule. Because the tier is premium, the PremiumFeeStrategy is selected from the Map and it computes half a percent of fifty thousand, which is two hundred and fifty rupees. The fee value now exists as a BigDecimal; account balances are still untouched.

Step 4 — The Circuit Breaker guarded FX client is asked for a reference USD/INR rate. The breaker is closed, so the call succeeds and returns eighty-three point three zero. If the provider had failed three times, the breaker would have opened and returned the cached rate of eighty-three point two five instead. This step does not change balances; it only demonstrates the protected external call.

Step 5 — The money actually moves. Rajesh is debited the amount plus the fee, so fifty thousand two hundred and fifty rupees leaves his account and his balance becomes nine lakh forty-nine thousand seven hundred and fifty rupees. Priya is credited the amount, so fifty thousand rupees arrive and her balance becomes three lakh rupees.

Step 6 — The Observer pattern fires. A single TransferCompletedEvent is published, and both listeners react independently: the audit listener writes the audit line and the notification listener writes the SMS line. Neither the balances nor the result object change here; this step is purely the side-effects fanning out.

Step 7 — The Builder assembles the immutable TransferResult with id TXF-00001, the from and to accounts, the amount, the fee, and the status COMPLETED. This object is returned to the caller as the final output.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In our banking transfer service I lean on a small set of design patterns that every production team expects you to know, and I always tie each one back to a concrete problem. The Strategy pattern handles fee calculation: instead of a giant if-else over customer tiers, I define a FeeStrategy interface with one implementation per rule and register them in a map keyed by tier. When marketing launches a festival zero-fee promotion, I add one class and one map entry, and I never touch the live transfer logic. That is the Open/Closed Principle in action.

The Builder pattern builds the transfer result object cleanly. A result has an id, a from-account, a to-account, an amount, a fee, a status, and a timestamp, and setting those by name in a chain removed a whole class of bugs where the from and to accounts used to get swapped in a long constructor. The object comes out immutable, which is exactly what you want for something that represents a completed money movement.

The Observer pattern keeps the core money-movement code clean. When a transfer completes I publish a single event, and independent listeners for audit, SMS, and the dashboard each react on their own. Adding a new reaction, like a fraud re-check, is just a new listener and never destabilises the part of the code that actually moves money. Alongside it, the Circuit Breaker pattern protects us from a flaky external rate provider: after a few failures it opens, stops hammering the sick service, and instantly returns the last cached rate, so one slow dependency can never freeze the whole service.

Finally, the DTO pattern protects the API boundary. Our account row carries an internal version column and a risk score that customers must never see, so the controller always returns a trimmed response record built from the entity. Underneath all of this sits SOLID: each class has a single responsibility, the service depends on interfaces rather than concrete classes so I can inject mocks in unit tests, and the strategy registry gives me Open/Closed and Dependency Inversion at the same time. When I describe this to an interviewer I make the point that these patterns are not decoration — each one removed a specific, real pain in a system that moves customer money every day.

sections.s2_technical:
Let me walk through each concept the way an experienced engineer would explain it to a junior joining the team, with a small finance code snippet for each so you can see the API actually being used.

REST is an architectural style where every piece of data is a resource with a clean URL, and you act on it using the standard HTTP methods. GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces the whole thing, PATCH updates part of it, and DELETE removes it. The important senior-level nuance is that the status code is part of your API contract. A created resource returns 201, a successful delete with no body returns 204, a missing resource returns 404, and a bad input returns 400. For example, a controller that creates a fund purchase marks itself as returning Created: `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)` on the method, so Spring sends 201 automatically instead of the default 200.

Error handling in modern Spring uses RFC 9457 ProblemDetail, which is a standard JSON shape for errors so every client can parse failures the same way. Instead of returning a random map, you build a ProblemDetail: `ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Fund not found: FND-999");` and you can attach extra fields with `pd.setProperty("errors", list)`. The response then carries a title, a status, and a detail that a frontend can show directly to Rajesh.

Pagination at scale should use cursor (keyset) pagination rather than offset. Offset pagination with `OFFSET 100000` forces the database to count and throw away one hundred thousand rows before returning the next page, which gets slower the deeper you go. Cursor pagination remembers the last id seen and queries forward from it: `SELECT f FROM Fund f WHERE f.fundId > :cursor ORDER BY f.fundId`. Because fundId is indexed, the database seeks straight to that point, so page ten thousand is as fast as page one.

The Strategy pattern lets you swap an algorithm at runtime through a common interface. Instead of a long if-else chain for fee types, you define `FeeStrategy` with a `calculateFee` method and keep each variant in its own class. You then store them in a Map and pick one by name: `FeeStrategy s = feeStrategies.get("premium"); BigDecimal fee = s.calculateFee(amount);`. Adding a new fee type means writing one new class and adding one Map entry, with zero changes to existing code.

The Builder pattern constructs complex objects step by step so you avoid a constructor with fifteen arguments. For a trade you might write `Trade.builder().tradeId("T1").symbol("RELIANCE").amount(new BigDecimal("50000")).build()`, which reads clearly and lets optional fields be skipped. The Observer pattern decouples an event from its reactions: when a purchase settles, you publish one event and several independent listeners (audit, SMS, dashboard) react, so adding a new reaction never touches the settlement code. In Spring this is `applicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(new PurchaseSettledEvent(id))` with `@EventListener` methods consuming it.

SOLID is the five design rules. Single Responsibility means each class does one job, so FundService lists funds and a separate FeeStrategy only computes fees. Open/Closed means the system is open to new behavior but closed to editing working code, which the strategy Map achieves. Liskov Substitution means any FeeStrategy implementation works wherever the interface is expected. Interface Segregation means you keep interfaces small and focused rather than forcing classes to implement methods they do not need. Dependency Inversion means FundService depends on the FeeStrategy interface, not on a concrete class, which is why you can inject a mock strategy in a unit test: `new FundService(em, Map.of("regular", new RegularFeeStrategy()))`.

On the advanced Java side, sealed classes restrict exactly which types may implement an interface. Declaring `public sealed interface FeeStrategy permits RegularFeeStrategy, PremiumFeeStrategy, ZeroFeeStrategy` tells the compiler the complete list, so a switch over the type is exhaustive and needs no default branch. Records give you immutable data carriers with no boilerplate: `public record FundResponse(String fundId, String name, BigDecimal nav) {}` automatically generates the constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, and toString, which is ideal for DTOs. Pattern matching lets you test and bind a type in one step, for example `if (category instanceof FundCategory.Equity e) { ... }` or a switch that matches each permitted subtype directly. Reflection and the JPMS module system round out the advanced topics: reflection inspects classes at runtime, which is how frameworks like Spring and Jackson read your annotations, while modules declare explicit boundaries about what a jar exports.
sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the real situation at National Bank of India before we look at any code, the way I would explain it to a friend who understands banking but not Java.

The bank has launched an online mutual fund marketplace. Customers like Rajesh, a software engineer with savings account SAV2001, and Priya, a property owner with current account CUR3001, log in to browse funds and invest their money. The bank offers several funds: equity funds, debt funds, liquid funds, and tax-saving ELSS funds. This marketplace must feel fast, must never crash on bad input, and must charge the right fee to the right customer.

Problem 1 — The bank keeps adding new funds, and the fund list is getting very long. When Priya scrolls to page five hundred of the fund list, the old system becomes painfully slow because the database is counting and discarding all the earlier rows every time. This is exactly the problem cursor pagination solves: instead of skipping rows by number, the system remembers the last fund id shown and fetches the next batch starting just after it, so deep pages load instantly.

Problem 2 — Different customers deserve different fees. A regular customer pays one percent, a premium customer like Rajesh pays only half a percent, and during a festival promotion some customers pay nothing. The old code was one giant tangle of if-else statements, and every new offer meant editing that working code and risking a bug in the live fee calculation. This is exactly what the Strategy pattern fixes: each fee rule becomes its own small class behind a common interface, and the service simply looks up the right one by name. A new promotion is a new class plus one line in a map, with the existing fee logic left untouched.

Problem 3 — Customers sometimes send bad requests: a fund id that does not exist, or an amount below the minimum. If the system returns messy or inconsistent errors, the mobile app cannot show a clear message and support calls go up. This is exactly why we use RFC 9457 ProblemDetail: every error comes back in the same structured shape with a title, a status, and a detail, so the app always knows how to display it to the customer.

Problem 4 — The team wants the code to be safe and future-proof. Fund categories and fee types should be a fixed, known set so nobody accidentally introduces a rogue category, and the data objects sent back to customers should be impossible to tamper with after creation. This is exactly what sealed classes and records provide: sealed interfaces lock the list of allowed fee strategies and fund categories so the compiler enforces completeness, and records make the response objects immutable.

Now that the problems are clear, here is what each part of the code will do. The FundCategory sealed interface defines the fixed set of fund categories with their maximum expense ratios. The FeeStrategy sealed interface defines the fee contract, with RegularFeeStrategy, PremiumFeeStrategy, and ZeroFeeStrategy as the three permitted implementations. The FeeStrategyConfig class registers these three strategies in a Map so the service can pick one by name. The Fund entity maps to the funds table in the database. The FundResponse record is the safe DTO we return instead of the raw entity, and PurchaseRequest and PageResponse are the request and paginated response records. The FundNotFoundException and GlobalExceptionHandler classes turn failures into clean ProblemDetail responses. The FundService class holds the business logic: getFund reads a single fund, listFunds does cursor pagination, and calculateFee runs the chosen strategy. The FundController exposes these as REST endpoints with correct HTTP methods and status codes. Finally, FundServiceTest proves each fee strategy produces the right number.

sections.s5_journey:
The input data is a purchase request that Rajesh sends from his mobile app. He wants to buy units of the NBI Bluechip Equity fund (FND-001) for one lakh rupees, and because he is a premium customer he qualifies for the premium fee strategy. The raw request looks like this JSON body: `{"accountId":"SAV2001","fundId":"FND-001","amount":100000,"feeStrategy":"premium"}` sent to `POST /api/v1/funds/FND-001/purchase`.

Step 1: The request arrives at the controller. Spring reads the JSON body and converts it into a PurchaseRequest record. At this moment the data lives in memory as an immutable Java object with accountId "SAV2001", fundId "FND-001", amount 100000 as a BigDecimal, and feeStrategy "premium". The `@Valid` annotation checks the rules: accountId is not blank, fundId is not blank, and amount is at least 100. All checks pass, so the request moves forward unchanged.

Step 2: The controller calls `fundService.getFund("FND-001")`. The service asks the EntityManager to find the Fund entity with that id. The data now crosses from the service into PostgreSQL. The database returns one row, which Hibernate turns into a Fund entity holding the name "NBI Bluechip Equity", a NAV of 45.2300, and an expense ratio. If no row existed, the service would throw FundNotFoundException and the journey would end at a 404 ProblemDetail response. The fund exists, so the entity is converted into a FundResponse record so the raw entity is never exposed outside the service.

Step 3: The controller calls `fundService.calculateFee("premium", 100000)`. Inside the service the feeStrategies Map is consulted. The key "premium" maps to the PremiumFeeStrategy object. The amount stays the same, one lakh rupees, but now it flows into the strategy. The PremiumFeeStrategy multiplies 100000 by its rate of 0.005 and sets the scale to two decimals using HALF_UP rounding, producing a new BigDecimal of 500.00. The original amount is unchanged; the fee is a brand new value derived from it.

Step 4: The controller builds the confirmation message. It combines the fund name from Step 2, the purchase amount from Step 1, and the computed fee from Step 3 into a single human-readable string. The data has now been transformed from raw JSON into a meaningful business result.

Step 5: Spring serializes the result and sends it back with HTTP status 201 Created because a new purchase was recorded. The response leaves the service, passes back through the gateway, and lands in Rajesh's app. The final output looks like this:

```
Oct 25, 2026 9:12:04 PM com.bank.marketplace.service.FundService calculateFee
INFO: Fee: 100000 → Rs.500.00 (strategy: Premium (0.5%))

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: text/plain
Purchased Rs.100000 of NBI Bluechip Equity (fee: Rs.500.00 via premium strategy)
```

  POST   /api/v1/funds/{id}/purchase → 201 Created

sections.s5c_hld:
High-Level Design is the bird's-eye view of the whole system. Imagine standing on the rooftop of the National Bank of India head office and looking down at the entire operation. You do not see individual desks or forms — you see the big departments and how requests travel between them. For this mutual fund marketplace, the big departments are: the customers who open the app, the front door that checks their identity, the services that actually process fund purchases, the fast memory that remembers fund prices, the permanent vault that stores every record, the postal system that passes messages between services, the outside agencies the bank must talk to, and the cameras and alarms that watch everything.

The client layer is where a request begins. A customer called Rajesh opens the banking app on his phone, or a web browser, or an automated SIP (systematic investment plan) scheduler fires at 9 AM to buy fund units automatically. All of these send an HTTPS request toward the bank.

The API Gateway is the front door with a security guard. It terminates SSL, checks Rajesh's JWT token to confirm he is really Rajesh, rate-limits how many purchase requests one account can fire per second so nobody can flood the system, and then routes the request to the correct service. Without this door, an attacker could hammer the purchase endpoint or an unauthenticated stranger could read fund data.

The application layer is the brain. The Fund Service validates the purchase, picks the correct fee strategy at runtime, and records the order. It is stateless and runs as multiple copies behind the gateway, so if one copy is busy settling a large order, the others keep serving balance lookups. Services talk synchronously over REST when they need an immediate answer, and asynchronously over Kafka when the work can happen later, such as sending Rajesh a confirmation SMS.

The caching layer is Redis. Fund NAV (net asset value) prices and fund metadata are read thousands of times per second but change only a few times a day, so the service reads them from Redis in microseconds instead of hitting PostgreSQL every time. A short time-to-live keeps the cached price fresh.

The data layer is PostgreSQL, the permanent source of truth holding the funds and purchase records. Heavy reporting reads go to a read replica so analytics never slow down live purchases. The message queue layer is Kafka: when a purchase completes, the service drops a "purchase completed" event into a topic and moves on, while audit and notification consumers pick it up independently. External systems include the RTA (registrar and transfer agent) such as CAMS or KFintech that actually allots fund units, and the UPI or NEFT payment rail that moves Rajesh's money. Observability (Prometheus, Grafana, ELK logs, Jaeger tracing, PagerDuty alerts) watches latency and errors, and the security layer enforces OAuth2 or JWT authentication, role-based authorization, TLS in transit, and encryption at rest because this is real money.

sections.s6_takeaway:
REST APIs follow resource-based URL design with proper HTTP methods and status codes: GET for reading, POST for creating with 201 Created, DELETE with 204 No Content. Error responses use RFC 9457 ProblemDetail for structured JSON. Cursor pagination (keyset) is fast for deep pages: the client sends the last seen ID and the query uses WHERE id > lastId with an index seek instead of OFFSET which scans and discards rows.

The Strategy pattern replaces if-else chains by mapping each variant to a named implementation in a Map. Adding a new fee strategy means creating a class and adding one Map entry — no existing code changes, satisfying the Open/Closed Principle. Sealed classes restrict which classes can implement an interface, enabling exhaustive switch expressions without a default case — the compiler ensures all subtypes are handled. Records provide immutable DTOs with auto-generated equals, hashCode, and toString — ideal for API response objects that should never be mutated after creation.

answers.question: What does REST stand for (Representational State Transfer, an architectural style — not a protocol — defined by Roy Fielding), what are its core constraints (client-server, statelessness, cacheability, layered system, uniform interface / resource-based URLs, optional code-on-demand, and HATEOAS), and how does a RESTful API differ from an RPC-style/"non-REST" HTTP API (resource nouns like `/users/123` + correct HTTP verbs vs action verbs like `/getUser`)?
answers.shortTitle: What does REST stand for, its core constraints, and how a RESTful API differs from RPC-style HTTP

s1_definition.profdef: REST stands for Representational State Transfer. It is an architectural style for building networked applications, defined by Roy Fielding in his 2000 doctoral dissertation. It is not a protocol or a standard — it is a set of constraints that, when applied over HTTP, produce scalable, cacheable, loosely coupled systems. The key constraints are client-server separation, statelessness, cacheability, a layered system, a uniform interface based on resources, optional code-on-demand, and hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS).
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India's online system as a very disciplined post office. Every account, every transaction, every customer is a "thing" (a resource) with its own address, like `/accounts/SAV2001` for Rajesh's savings account. To interact with a thing you use standard actions that everyone already understands: GET to read, POST to create, PUT to replace, DELETE to remove. An RPC-style system instead would have weird addresses like `/getRajeshBalance` and `/doTransferNow` — each one a custom verb nobody can guess. REST says: name the nouns, use the standard verbs.
s1_definition.oneliner: REST is resource-nouns plus standard HTTP verbs, stateless and cacheable — not custom action endpoints.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** REST stands for Representational State Transfer. It is an architectural style for building networked applications, defined by Roy Fielding in his 2000 doctoral dissertation. It is not a protocol or a standard — it is a set of constraints that, when applied over HTTP, produce scalable, cacheable, loosely coupled systems. The key constraints are client-server separation, statelessness, cacheability, a layered system, a uniform interface based on resources, optional code-on-demand, and hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India's online system as a very disciplined post office. Every account, every transaction, every customer is a "thing" (a resource) with its own address, like `/accounts/SAV2001` for Rajesh's savings account. To interact with a thing you use standard actions that everyone already understands: GET to read, POST to create, PUT to replace, DELETE to remove. An RPC-style system instead would have weird addresses like `/getRajeshBalance` and `/doTransferNow` — each one a custom verb nobody can guess. REST says: name the nouns, use the standard verbs.

**One line to remember:** REST is resource-nouns plus standard HTTP verbs, stateless and cacheable — not custom action endpoints.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India is building a new account service. The old system had endpoints like `/getBalance`, `/createAccount`, and `/removeAccount`. Every new mobile app developer had to read a 40-page document just to learn the endpoint names, because none of them followed a pattern. This is exactly the problem REST solves. By naming resources `/accounts/{id}` and using GET, POST, and DELETE, a developer who has never seen the API can guess that `GET /accounts/SAV2001` reads Rajesh's account.

Problem 2 — The old system stored a server-side session. When traffic grew, the bank added a second server, but Rajesh's session lived only on server one, so when the load balancer sent his next request to server two, he was logged out. This is exactly what statelessness fixes. If every request carries the JWT token, either server can serve Rajesh, and the bank can add ten servers without session trouble.

Problem 3 — The balance screen was hammering the database because the app re-fetched the balance every second. This is where cacheability helps. By returning a `Cache-Control` header, the balance can be safely reused for a short window, cutting database load.

We will build a small Spring Boot account service that demonstrates proper REST design. It will have an `Account` entity for Rajesh and Priya, an `AccountController` exposing resource-based endpoints with correct verbs, an `AccountService` holding the logic, cache headers on the read endpoint, stateless handling (token on each request, no session), and a comparison showing the RPC-style anti-pattern we are avoiding. The demo traces a GET for Rajesh's account and a POST creating a transfer.

Input data: a GET request for `/api/v1/accounts/SAV2001` with an Authorization header carrying Rajesh's JWT.

Step 1: The request arrives at the server. Because REST is stateless, the server does not look up any session. It reads the JWT token from the header to know this is Rajesh. Everything needed is in the request itself.

Step 2: Spring routes the URL `/api/v1/accounts/SAV2001` to `AccountController.getAccount`, extracting `SAV2001` as the path variable. The noun in the URL identifies the resource.

Step 3: The controller calls `service.findById("SAV2001")`. The service returns Rajesh's account with balance one million rupees.

Step 4: The controller builds an `AccountResponse` representation — only the safe fields, not the raw entity — and attaches a `Cache-Control: max-age=30` header, making the response cacheable for thirty seconds.

Step 5: The client receives `200 OK` with the JSON representation. If Rajesh's app asks again within thirty seconds, a cache can answer without touching the server, reducing load.

sections.s6_takeaway:
REST stands for Representational State Transfer. It is an architectural style defined by Roy Fielding, not a protocol, and it is built on a set of constraints: client-server separation, statelessness, cacheability, a layered system, a uniform interface, optional code-on-demand, and hypermedia as the engine of application state. When these constraints are applied over HTTP, you get a system that scales well, caches naturally, and stays loosely coupled.

The most important idea is the uniform interface. In REST you model your system as resources, which are the meaningful business things, and you give each a stable URL made of nouns. In my banking work at National Bank of India, reading an account is a GET on `/accounts/SAV2001`, creating a transfer is a POST to the `/transfers` collection, and removing a beneficiary is a DELETE on `/beneficiaries/BEN-77`. The HTTP verb carries the action, so a developer who has never seen the API can still guess what each endpoint does.

Statelessness is what let us scale. Because every request carries its own JWT token and all the data it needs, the server keeps no session memory, so any of our three service instances can serve any request. We added servers freely without worrying about sticky sessions. Cacheability came from returning a Cache-Control header on the balance read, so the mobile app could reuse a balance for thirty seconds instead of hammering the database.

The difference from an RPC-style HTTP API is sharp. RPC puts actions in the URL, like `/getBalance` or `/doTransfer`, treats HTTP as a dumb tunnel, and often returns 200 even for errors. REST uses resource nouns, the correct verbs, and the correct status codes, so the whole ecosystem of proxies, caches, and monitoring tools understands it without custom logic. That is why, when someone says their API is REST just because it returns JSON, I check whether they actually use resource URLs, proper verbs, and status codes, because that is what REST really means.

---

answers.question: What are the roles of the HTTP methods in RESTful APIs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS)?
answers.shortTitle: What are the roles of the HTTP methods in RESTful APIs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS)

s1_definition.profdef: HTTP methods, also called verbs, tell the server what action to perform on a resource identified by a URL. In REST, GET reads a resource, POST creates a new resource under a collection, PUT fully replaces a resource, PATCH partially updates it, DELETE removes it, HEAD fetches only the headers of a GET without the body, and OPTIONS reports which methods a resource supports. Each verb has defined semantics around safety and idempotency that clients, caches, and proxies rely on.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's records room. GET is "show me Rajesh's file" — you only look, nothing changes. POST is "open a new transfer slip" — a fresh record is created. PUT is "replace Priya's entire profile form with this new one." PATCH is "just change Priya's phone number, leave the rest." DELETE is "shred this beneficiary record." HEAD is "does Rajesh's file exist and how big is it?" without pulling the whole file. OPTIONS is "which actions am I allowed to do on this file?"
s1_definition.oneliner: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes, HEAD checks, OPTIONS asks what is allowed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** HTTP methods, also called verbs, tell the server what action to perform on a resource identified by a URL. In REST, GET reads a resource, POST creates a new resource under a collection, PUT fully replaces a resource, PATCH partially updates it, DELETE removes it, HEAD fetches only the headers of a GET without the body, and OPTIONS reports which methods a resource supports. Each verb has defined semantics around safety and idempotency that clients, caches, and proxies rely on.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's records room. GET is "show me Rajesh's file" — you only look, nothing changes. POST is "open a new transfer slip" — a fresh record is created. PUT is "replace Priya's entire profile form with this new one." PATCH is "just change Priya's phone number, leave the rest." DELETE is "shred this beneficiary record." HEAD is "does Rajesh's file exist and how big is it?" without pulling the whole file. OPTIONS is "which actions am I allowed to do on this file?"

**One line to remember:** GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes, HEAD checks, OPTIONS asks what is allowed.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's beneficiary feature originally did everything through one `POST /updateBeneficiary` endpoint. When Priya wanted to change only her landlord's nickname, the app had to send the entire beneficiary object, and a bug once wiped out the account number because one field was accidentally left blank. This is exactly why PUT and PATCH are different verbs. PUT means "replace the whole thing," so a missing field legitimately clears it, whereas PATCH means "change only what I send," which is what Priya actually wanted.

Problem 2 — The mobile app downloaded a full 2 MB PDF statement just to show whether a statement was available for a month, wasting data on a slow connection. This is exactly what HEAD solves. A HEAD request returns the headers, including size and existence, without the 2 MB body.

Problem 3 — The web portal, running on a different domain, kept getting blocked by the browser when calling the transfer API. This is where OPTIONS matters, because the browser sends an OPTIONS preflight to check whether the cross-origin POST is allowed before sending it.

We will build a beneficiary service that demonstrates every verb: GET to read a beneficiary, POST to create one, PUT to fully replace one, PATCH to partially update a nickname, DELETE to remove one, HEAD to check a statement, and OPTIONS to report allowed methods. The demo walks through Priya creating, reading, patching, and deleting a beneficiary.

Input data: Priya creates a beneficiary, reads it, patches only the nickname, then deletes it.

Step 1: Priya's app sends `POST /api/v1/beneficiaries/BEN-88` with the full body. The service stores a new Beneficiary and the controller returns `201 Created` with a Location header. A fresh resource now exists.

Step 2: The app sends `GET /api/v1/beneficiaries/BEN-88`. This is safe, so nothing changes. The server returns `200 OK` with the full beneficiary. Calling it ten times returns the same answer because GET is idempotent.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In a RESTful API every HTTP method has a defined role and defined properties around safety and idempotency. GET reads a resource and is both safe and idempotent, meaning it never changes server state and can be called repeatedly with the same result, which also makes it cacheable. POST creates a new resource under a collection and is neither safe nor idempotent, so two identical POSTs normally create two resources, which is why I return 201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new resource.

PUT and PATCH are both updates but they mean different things. PUT is a full replacement and is idempotent, so if a client omits a field, PUT semantics say that field is cleared, because PUT means this is the entire resource now. PATCH is a partial update where the client sends only the fields to change. In my beneficiary work at National Bank of India, when Priya wanted to change only the nickname of her landlord beneficiary, PATCH was the right verb, because sending a PUT with a missing account number would have wiped out that field.

DELETE removes a resource and is idempotent, so deleting something already deleted still leaves it deleted, and I usually return 204 No Content with an empty body. HEAD behaves exactly like GET but returns only headers with no body, which we used so the mobile app could check whether a statement existed and how large it was without downloading a two megabyte PDF. OPTIONS reports which methods a resource supports through the Allow header, and it is also what the browser uses for CORS preflight before a cross-origin POST.

The reason these properties matter beyond theory is retry behaviour. A proxy or client may safely retry a GET, PUT, or DELETE after a network glitch because repeating them is harmless, but it must never blindly retry a POST, because that could create a duplicate transfer and move Rajesh's money twice. So choosing the correct verb is not cosmetic — it directly protects correctness when the network is unreliable, which in a banking system is exactly where correctness matters most.

---

answers.question: What are idempotent methods, and which HTTP methods are idempotent (and why)?
answers.shortTitle: What are idempotent methods, and which HTTP methods are idempotent (and why)

s1_definition.profdef: An HTTP method is idempotent when making the same request one time or many times leaves the server in the same final state. The response to the client may differ, but the server-side effect is identical. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent. POST and PATCH are generally not idempotent. Idempotency is what lets clients and intermediaries safely retry a request after a timeout without causing duplicate side effects.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh presses an elevator button at National Bank of India. Pressing it once or ten times calls the elevator to the same floor — that is idempotent. Now imagine the "transfer 50,000 rupees" button. Pressing it ten times moves 500,000 rupees — that is not idempotent, and it is dangerous. Idempotent actions are the ones where repeating the press changes nothing extra, so if Rajesh is not sure whether the first press registered, he can press again without fear.
s1_definition.oneliner: Idempotent means repeating the request does not change the final result, so it is safe to retry — GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE qualify; POST and PATCH usually do not.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An HTTP method is idempotent when making the same request one time or many times leaves the server in the same final state. The response to the client may differ, but the server-side effect is identical. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent. POST and PATCH are generally not idempotent. Idempotency is what lets clients and intermediaries safely retry a request after a timeout without causing duplicate side effects.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh presses an elevator button at National Bank of India. Pressing it once or ten times calls the elevator to the same floor — that is idempotent. Now imagine the "transfer 50,000 rupees" button. Pressing it ten times moves 500,000 rupees — that is not idempotent, and it is dangerous. Idempotent actions are the ones where repeating the press changes nothing extra, so if Rajesh is not sure whether the first press registered, he can press again without fear.

**One line to remember:** Idempotent means repeating the request does not change the final result, so it is safe to retry — GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE qualify; POST and PATCH usually do not.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh taps "Transfer 50,000 to Priya" on the National Bank of India app. His phone is on a weak signal, the response never arrives, and the app shows a spinner. Rajesh taps again. If the transfer endpoint is a plain POST with no protection, the bank now has two transfers and Priya receives 100,000 rupees. This is exactly the danger of a non-idempotent method under retry, and it is why we need an idempotency key.

Problem 2 — A background job retries failed requests automatically. For reading balances with GET, retrying is perfectly safe because GET is idempotent. For deleting a stale beneficiary with DELETE, retrying is also safe because the end state is identical. The job can retry these freely. This shows why knowing which verbs are idempotent lets us build safe automatic retry logic.

Problem 3 — The app lets Priya update her full profile with PUT. Even if the PUT is sent twice because of a flaky connection, her profile ends identical both times, so no harm is done. This demonstrates PUT idempotency in practice.

We will build a transfer service where POST is made safe using an idempotency key stored in a map, so a repeated key returns the original transfer instead of creating a new one. We will also show a GET read, a PUT profile update, and a DELETE, and a demo that sends the same POST twice with the same key to prove only one transfer happens while sending GET twice proves it is naturally safe.

Input data: Rajesh sends two identical POSTs to transfer 50,000 rupees to Priya, both carrying the same Idempotency-Key `11112222-3333`, because his first tap seemed to fail.

Step 1: The first POST arrives. The service looks up the key in its map and finds nothing. This is a new transfer.

Step 2: The service creates transfer TXF-abc12345, records it under the key, and performs the single debit and credit. Rajesh's balance goes from one million to 950,000 and Priya's from 250,000 to 300,000. The response has `replayed=false`.

Step 3: The second POST arrives with the same key because Rajesh tapped again. The service looks up the key and this time finds the existing transfer.

Step 4: Because the key already exists, the service does not create anything and does not move money again. It returns the original transfer with `replayed=true`. Balances are untouched by this second call.

Step 5: The net effect is exactly one transfer of 50,000 rupees even though two requests were sent. This is how we retrofit idempotency onto POST, which is not idempotent by default.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 21:40:00 INFO  POST /transfers key=11112222-3333 -> TXF-abc12345 replayed=false (money moved once)
2026-10-25 21:40:02 INFO  POST /transfers key=11112222-3333 -> TXF-abc12345 replayed=true  (no new transfer)
Rajesh SAV2001: 1,000,000 -> 950,000 (changed only once)
Priya  CUR3001:   250,000 -> 300,000 (changed only once)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
An HTTP method is idempotent when sending the same request one time or many times leaves the server in the same final state. The important detail is that idempotency is about server state, not the response, so a DELETE that returns 204 the first time and 404 the second is still idempotent because the resource ends deleted either way. The idempotent methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, and DELETE, while POST and PATCH are generally not idempotent.

The reasoning behind each is straightforward. GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS only read, so repeating them changes nothing. PUT is a full replacement, so writing the same complete representation twice ends in the same state. DELETE leaves the resource gone whether called once or ten times. POST is not idempotent because it normally creates a new resource each time, and PATCH is not idempotent in general because a PATCH like add one hundred to the balance would stack up on repeats.

The reason this matters in a banking system is retries under unreliable networks. In my work at National Bank of India, when Rajesh tapped transfer on a weak signal and the response timed out, his app could not tell whether the money had moved, so it retried. If the transfer endpoint were a plain POST, that retry would have created a second transfer and moved fifty thousand rupees twice. Because POST is not idempotent by the specification, we added an idempotency key: the client sends a unique key in a header, the server records it, and a repeat of the same key returns the original transfer instead of executing a new one.

So in practice I let intermediaries and background jobs retry GET, PUT, and DELETE freely because they are naturally idempotent, and I deliberately retrofit idempotency onto POST using an idempotency key whenever the operation moves money or has any side effect that must happen exactly once. That combination is what keeps the system both resilient to network failures and correct about never double-charging a customer.

answers.question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
answers.shortTitle: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH

s1_definition.profdef: PUT and PATCH both update a resource, but they differ in scope and semantics. PUT performs a full replacement: the client sends the complete representation and the server replaces the entire resource, so any field the client omits is set to its default or cleared. PATCH performs a partial update: the client sends only the fields to change, and the server leaves every other field untouched. PUT is idempotent by definition; PATCH is not guaranteed idempotent.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of Priya's profile form at National Bank of India. PUT is like handing the clerk a brand new, fully filled form that completely replaces the old one — if you left the phone number blank on the new form, the clerk erases the old phone number too, because the new form is now the truth. PATCH is like handing the clerk a sticky note that says "only change the phone number to this" — everything else on the existing form stays exactly as it was.
s1_definition.oneliner: PUT replaces the whole resource (missing fields get cleared); PATCH changes only the fields you send (everything else stays).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** PUT and PATCH both update a resource, but they differ in scope and semantics. PUT performs a full replacement: the client sends the complete representation and the server replaces the entire resource, so any field the client omits is set to its default or cleared. PATCH performs a partial update: the client sends only the fields to change, and the server leaves every other field untouched. PUT is idempotent by definition; PATCH is not guaranteed idempotent.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of Priya's profile form at National Bank of India. PUT is like handing the clerk a brand new, fully filled form that completely replaces the old one — if you left the phone number blank on the new form, the clerk erases the old phone number too, because the new form is now the truth. PATCH is like handing the clerk a sticky note that says "only change the phone number to this" — everything else on the existing form stays exactly as it was.

**One line to remember:** PUT replaces the whole resource (missing fields get cleared); PATCH changes only the fields you send (everything else stays).

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Priya saved a beneficiary at National Bank of India with an account number, a nickname, and an IFSC code. She only wanted to rename the nickname from Rajesh to Landlord. The app sent the change through an endpoint that behaved like PUT but only included the nickname, and the account number and IFSC were wiped out, so her next rent payment failed. This is exactly the difference between PUT and PATCH. PUT replaces everything, so omitting the account number cleared it, whereas PATCH would have changed only the nickname.

Problem 2 — The bank also needs a way to replace a full profile when a customer re-submits their complete KYC form. Here PUT is correct, because the new form is meant to completely supersede the old one, and idempotency means re-submitting the same form twice is harmless.

Problem 3 — A retry mechanism re-sends updates after timeouts. For PUT this is safe because it is idempotent. For PATCH that expresses relative changes it is not safe, so the team must be careful which verb they let the retry layer resend.

We will build a beneficiary service with both a PUT endpoint that fully replaces and a PATCH endpoint that only updates provided fields. The demo shows Priya doing a PATCH on only the nickname, proving the account number survives, and then a PUT with a missing field, proving that field gets cleared.

Step 4: Now suppose Priya instead sent a PUT with only `{"nickname":"Landlord"}`. sections.s6_takeaway:
PUT and PATCH both update a resource but they mean very different things. PUT is a full replacement: the client sends the complete representation, and the server replaces the entire resource, so any field the client leaves out is cleared or set to default, because PUT says this body is the whole resource now. PATCH is a partial update: the client sends only the fields it wants to change, and the server leaves every other field exactly as it was.

A direct consequence is idempotency. PUT is idempotent because sending the same full body twice ends in the same state both times, which makes it safe to retry after a timeout. PATCH is not guaranteed idempotent, because a PATCH that expresses a relative change like add one hundred to the balance would stack up if repeated, so I treat PATCH as non-idempotent unless I specifically designed it with absolute values.

In my beneficiary work at National Bank of India this distinction prevented a real bug. Priya wanted to change only the nickname of her saved landlord beneficiary. When the app sent only the nickname through an endpoint that behaved like PUT, the account number and IFSC were wiped out because PUT treats missing fields as cleared, and her next rent payment failed. The fix was to use PATCH for partial edits so only the nickname changed and the other fields survived, and to reserve PUT for cases where the customer genuinely re-submits a complete form such as full KYC.

The careful detail I always mention is validation and null handling. For PUT I validate the full object because every field must be present, while for PATCH I validate only the fields that are present. And because a simple ignore-nulls merge cannot tell the difference between change this to null and do not touch this, I either document that null means skip, or I adopt JSON Merge Patch where null means delete, or JSON Patch for fully explicit operations. Choosing the right verb and being precise about missing fields is what keeps partial updates safe in a banking API.
